item.title: PrimeXBT’s PXTrader 2.0 platform: 5 Features to Check Out Before Your Next Trade
item.description:
Wouldn’t it be cool if your trading platform gave you more ways to put your ideas into action and explore new opportunities across markets?

 

PrimeXBT, a global multi-asset broker and crypto asset service provider, brings that flexibility and innovation to its native PXTrader 2.0 platform. Designed for beginners and experienced traders alike, it combines intuitive navigation with advanced analysis and risk management tools for Crypto Futures, Forex and CFD trading.

 

Here are five practical features worth checking out before your next trade.

 

1. Using crypto to trade traditional markets

 

PXTrader 2.0 supports accounts in USD, USDT, USDC, BTC and ETH, allowing clients to use Bitcoin or Ethereum as trading capital for Forex and CFDs on indices, commodities and shares.

 

Earnings season is one example of when this flexibility can come into play, allowing crypto traders to participate using their existing holdings. A client holding ETH, for instance, can trade share CFDs as markets react to company results and outlooks, without first converting their funds into fiat. The position reflects movements in the underlying share price, while the account remains denominated in Ethereum. Changes in ETH’s price also affect the fiat value of the account balance.

 

Clients holding other supported cryptocurrencies can use PrimeXBT’s built-in exchange feature to swap them for a supported account currency. PrimeXBT also offers over 100 payment methods, including fiat and crypto options alongside a wide selection of local payment solutions.

 

2. Trading Crypto Futures and CFDs from one account

 

A change in interest-rate expectations can influence currencies, equities, gold and crypto at the same time. For traders following these connections, access to several asset classes makes it possible to compare how different markets respond to the same development.

 

PXTrader 2.0 combines Crypto Futures and CFDs within one trading account. Clients can follow a view across different instruments and manage related positions without moving funds between separate Futures and CFD accounts.

 

Integrated TradingView charts provide more than 100 technical indicators alongside drawing tools and chart-based trading. This lets traders compare price action and prepare orders within the same workspace, using a consistent set of analysis tools across markets.

 

3. Accessing gold throughout the weekend

 

A geopolitical event or unexpected political announcement can change a trader’s outlook while conventional markets are closed. PXTrader 2.0’s GOLD 24/7 instrument extends access to gold throughout the week, including Saturdays and Sundays.

 

Traders can open a GOLD 24/7 position in response to new information, adjust their exposure or close an existing trade if their assessment changes. This gives them an opportunity to manage those positions ahead of the standard gold market’s reopening, when weekend developments can trigger price gaps.

 

4. Setting up risk and position controls around the strategy

 

The way a position is configured determines how it uses margin and interacts with other trades. PXTrader 2.0 provides several controls that traders can review before placing an order.

 

Adjustable leverage lets clients set maximum leverage limits. Real-time margin tracking and visible estimated liquidation levels help traders monitor exposure. Stop-loss and take-profit orders can be attached at entry, allowing traders to plan exit levels as part of the initial order.

 

Cross and Isolated margin offer different ways to allocate funds to supported positions. Cross margin uses the available account balance to support positions, while Isolated margin assigns margin to an individual position. The appropriate setting depends on how the trader wants to allocate capital and manage exposure.

 

Hedge and Netting modes address a separate decision: how trades on the same instrument are handled. Hedge mode allows separate long and short positions to remain open, while Netting mode combines trades into a single net position. Available margin and leverage settings depend on the selected mode.

 

Negative balance protection provides a further safeguard, preventing losing more than the funds available in the trading account.

 

5. Turning everyday trading into rewards

 

Clients can earn rewards from something they already do: trading. By completing tasks and reaching trading-volume milestones in PrimeXBT’s Rewards Center, they can build a rewards balance to use in three ways:

 

●       Cashback: recover up to 10% of eligible trading costs on PXTrader 2.0 as fully withdrawable cashback.

●       Trading Bonus: add trading credit to an account to increase the margin available for trading.

●       VIP status: unlock a VIP tier for 30 days to access lower trading fees and spreads.

 

New clients receive VIP 4 automatically for their first 14 days through the VIP Welcome offer. This includes up to 15% off Forex and CFD spreads, with reductions of up to 50% on Gold and Bitcoin CFD spreads, plus 33% off Crypto Futures taker fees. The offer also provides 10% off Exchange spreads and 24/7 priority support.

 

The full five-tier VIP program bases qualification on trading volume over the preceding 30 days. Depending on the tier, clients can access up to 25% off Forex and CFD spreads and Crypto Futures taker fees as low as 0.015%. VIP spread examples include Gold from $0.17, BTC/USD from $19, US500 from 0.2 points and USTEC from 0.4 points.

 

More ways to trade

 

PrimeXBT’s approach to innovation puts practical choice at the centre of the experience, giving clients greater flexibility in how they access markets, manage positions and use their trading capital. Whether a trader is funding a position with crypto, following a market theme across asset classes or preparing to trade gold over the weekend, its PXTrader 2.0 platform brings these possibilities together in one trading environment.

 

Start trading with PrimeXBT.

The platform bridges traditional and digital markets within one integrated environment, redefining versatility and innovation in online trading. Clients can access Forex, CFDs on indices, commodities, shares, crypto, and Crypto Futures, as well as buy, store and exchange cryptocurrencies. This unified experience extends across both the native PXTrader 2.0 platform and MetaTrader 5, supported by advanced risk-management tools and a wide range of funding options in crypto, fiat and local payment methods. item.title: Solana edges higher amid improved risk sentiment as immediate US-Iran escalation fears fade
item.description:
Solana extended the losses into a major support zone recently as fears of potential US strikes on Iran weighed on the crypto market. Those fears proved to be unfounded, and we’ve started to see risk sentiment improve as oil prices eased.

In the bigger picture, nothing has changed, with the Middle East crisis continuing to put upward pressure on inflation while weighing on global growth. The Federal Reserve is also being forced to maintain a tightening bias, while the upcoming US midterm elections add another layer of uncertainty. These headwinds are likely to limit any major rally in Solana.

This week, the focus will be on Wednesday’s FOMC decision and further developments in the Middle East.

The Fed is widely expected to keep interest rates unchanged, so a surprise rate hike would likely trigger a sharp selloff in Solana. We won’t get the Dot Plot at this meeting, so the attention will be on Fed Chair Warsh. Given his reluctance to provide forward guidance, though, he’s unlikely to say much, but traders will be watching closely for any hawkish surprises.

item.title: Connecting the dots: Why are Treasury yields falling as AI credit risks rise?
item.description:
As we get into the new week, Treasury yields are still sticking with the retreat from last week. 10-year yields are resting just below 5% today despite the fact that the inflation equation hasn't changed, as oil prices continue to push higher last week amid lingering tensions in the Middle East. And yet, tech stocks didn't exactly celebrate last week as the Nasdaq posted its first back-to-back weekly decline since July.

That sounds a little bid odd, doesn't it? Aren't lower bond yields supposed to be good for tech stocks?

Well, normally yes. However, I reckon that the story last week was more about where investors felt comfortable in putting their money. The question now is whether that story is going to keep up as we look to the weeks ahead.

Let's first dial it back and look at things more simply.

Imagine you have $100,000 to lend. One option is the US government, which is generally considered a relatively safe - if not the safest - borrower. The other choice is a tech firm that is spending billions in building data centres, hoping that those investments will eventually generate enough profits in the future.

A few months ago, investors might have been more enthusiastic about the second option. But with questions mounting over the enormous debt financing behind the AI boom, some investors are understandably becoming more cautious today. And we're seeing that reflected in the bond market.

10-year Treasury yields have now slipped back towards 5% even with oil prices remaining elevated and inflation concerns still lingering. Part of the story could be that investors are looking for the relative safety offered up by government bonds. And when more people buy Treasuries, their prices rise and yields fall.

However, I would argue that the money flow is what traders should be watching out for. While we are seeing more appetite to hold government debt in the past week, we're also seeing much more cautious conditions in terms of lending to companies heavily exposed to the AI boom.

But wait, how can we tell that? Well, you can see some of those nerves showing up in credit default swaps (CDS) which essentially measure how much investors are willing to pay for protection against a company failing to repay its debt.

For example, let's take a look at CoreWeave. Its five-year CDS surged above 1,000 bps earlier this month. Meanwhile, Oracle has also seen its CDS approach 300 bps. Put simply, investors are demanding much greater compensation for taking on the risk of lending to these companies.

Now, 1,000 bps might not sound like much but think about it this way. If you wanted to insure $1 million worth of CoreWeave's debt against default, it would cost you roughly $100,000 a year at that level. That's around 10% of the amount you're trying to protect, every single year.

When you put the dollar terms to that number, suddenly it turns out to be an awfully expensive insurance bill. And that tells us just how nervous investors have become about the company's ability to repay its debts.

For some context, Oracle's 300 bps would translate to roughly $30,000 a year for the same amount of protection. That's considerably less than CoreWeave, but still a sign of growing unease.

And considering how much money these tech companies are spending on AI infrastructure, one can understand why investors are starting to ask some really tough questions. After all, building data centres is one thing but generating enough profits to eventually pay back all that borrowed money is whole other thing.

Now, that is not to say the AI boom is suddenly falling apart. Demand for AI infrastructure remains strong and there's still plenty of money flowing in the space. However, it is clear that investors are starting to become more selective about which companies can justify those investments and, perhaps more importantly, which ones can afford to keep spending.

So, how does all of this tie back to falling Treasury yields?

The argument here is that we could be seeing some early signs of a shift in market sentiment. That is not to say that investors are abandoning risk altogether. However, they may be becoming less comfortable taking on certain types of risk - especially when it involves highly indebted AI companies.

And if that continues, it could create a rather dicey situation for tech stocks. Lower Treasury yields would ordinarily offer some support to valuations. But now, that benefit could be outweighed by growing concerns over corporate debt, financing costs and future profitability.

To keep things short, there's a big difference between yields falling because investors are optimistic about lower borrowing costs and yields falling because they're getting more worried about where else to put their money. And right now, there's a good chance that we are seeing the latter be part of the picture in broader markets.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: UK autumn budget preview: Can Healey calm markets and change BOE rate hike bets?
item.description:
The UK autumn budget is coming up on 28 October, just a week before the BOE's next monetary policy decision . And with inflation concerns still hanging over the economy, the government's fiscal plans could have a say in how interest rate expectations develop over the coming months.

For now, traders are pricing in roughly 99% odds of a 25 bps rate hike at the November meeting next week. So unless something really unexpected happens, that decision looks pretty much settled. As for December though, that is another story. Traders are currently pricing in around 47% odds of another rate hike before the year is out. That's essentially a coin toss and the autumn budget could be one to help tip expectations one way or the other.

So, what should traders be looking out for?

For starters, the general expectation is for a fairly cautious budget - one with modest tax increases and targeted support for households rather than any major spending commitments.

The backdrop is one where the government's fiscal headroom is looking rather uncomfortable. According to EY, that buffer against the government's fiscal rules has shrunk from £23.6 billion in March to an estimated £11.3 billion. That is largely because of higher borrowing costs and the economic fallout from the Iran conflict.

The latest Reuters survey suggests that Healey should try and rebuild that buffer to around £15-16 billion to reassure bond investors. So, that at least gives us some useful benchmark for judging the budget.

On taxes, Healey is possibly going to lean on an increase in the levy on bank profits as the main expected revenue-raising measure. There has also been speculation about extending the mansion tax to properties valued above £1.5 million, down from £2 million currently.

Meanwhile, targeted energy subsidies for lower-income households, relief on electricity bills and a possible extension of the fuel-duty cut are among the measures in focus. The question now is how much relief Healey can offer without adding to borrowing. After all, markets are already expecting a relatively restrained budget, so any larger-than-expected spending commitments could quickly raise concerns about how they will be funded.

Now, any measures that directly reduce household energy bills or fuel costs could also help ease near-term inflation pressures, thus potentially taking some pressure off the BOE. However, cash subsidies might simply end up bolstering household spending instead. So, the details and how the government intends to fund them will matter.

As for spending, Healey is expected to hold back on bigger commitments involving housebuilding, defence and public services, with many decisions potentially pushed into 2027. As such, that should offer some reassurance to gilt investors - provided that the government's borrowing forecasts also hold up.

In that regard, the OBR's updated forecasts on inflation, growth, and overall borrowing will also be heavily scrutinised as those projections will help markets judge whether the fiscal outlook is improving or deteriorating. If higher inflation and borrowing costs leave the fiscal outlook looking worse despite the government's restraint, then gilt yields could still come under pressure.

In looking at all of this, I would argue that the key for markets is trying to distinguish between yields rising because of inflation expectations and yields rising because investors are worried about fiscal credibility. The two angles carry very different implications for monetary policy in their own right.

A credible budget that limits borrowing, restrains demand and eases near-term energy inflation could encourage traders to scale back BOE rate hike bets for December and maybe next year. But if the fiscal package adds to inflation pressures, then markets could easily become more convinced that another rate hike is necessary.

Given what is priced in ahead of the budget, the November rate hike is largely a done deal and the bigger repricing opportunity lies with the December decision.

That being said, this is just one piece of the puzzle. UK inflation and labour market data will continue to be key factors in driving market expectations and they will continue to be major influences for the December outlook, as well as for the one next year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany Ifo business confidence improves in October as expectations surprise higher
item.description:
• Germany October Ifo business climate index 90.2 vs 90.0 expected
  • Prior 89.9
  • Germany October Ifo current conditions index 88.8 vs 89.9 expected
  • Prior 89.5
  • Germany October Ifo expectations index 91.6 vs 90.0 expected
  • Prior 90.4

The breakdownThe survey continues to reaffirm a further improvement in German business sentiment, one that is especially backed by stronger a stronger outlook for the months ahead. The current conditions index showed a decline in October but the expectations index surprisingly climbed to its highest since February 2022.

The latter is the standout here and reaffirms a more resilient setting for the German economy, even though recent PMI data has revealed some underlying weakness.

Still, the survey numbers here are not exactly hard data. So, we will have to see how this eventually transforms to the actual economic numbers in the months ahead to have a better sense of how well the economy might be holding up.

As such, I wouldn't get too carried away here. But at least for now, this is some welcome news after what the PMI numbers suggested for the euro area last week. The data won't do much to change the ECB decision this week though but we'll see how it fits among the trend in other data releases before the December meeting.

What does the data measure?The Ifo survey measures German business confidence, combining companies' assessments of current operating conditions with expectations for the next six months. It provides an early indication of economic activity, investment intentions and business sentiment.

Why does it matter to markets?Germany is Europe's largest economy, making its business sentiment an important barometer for the wider eurozone outlook. Changes in the expectations index especially can offer early clues about future economic growth, investment and employment.

How does this fit the broader economic picture?German business sentiment has improved for five consecutive months, with the headline index rising from 84.4 in April to 89.9 in September. The steady improvement in sentiment has been encouraging but last week's softer euro area PMI numbers suggest that growth momentum is slowing. A resilient Ifo reading would offer some reassurance, while a deterioration in expectations would raise further concerns about the recovery amid higher energy costs.

Current relevance to markets?Moderate. The release could influence euro and German bond market sentiment, especially if the expectations index surprises significantly. But with markets pricing in roughly 90% odds of no change at this week's ECB meeting, the report is more likely to provide additional economic context rather than trigger any meaningful policy repricing on its own.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What is the FOMC blackout period and why do central banks have one
item.description:
Central banks influence financial markets through both interest rate decisions and communication. Speeches and interviews can change expectations for future monetary policy, affecting bonds, currencies, equities and so on. To limit these signals immediately before policy decisions, many central banks have a blackout period.

A blackout period is a predefined period during which policymakers are restricted from publicly discussing monetary policy or the upcoming decision. The rules vary across central banks, but the purpose is to ensure that official announcements remain the primary source of information about the committee's decision.

The Federal Reserve's FOMC blackout period begins at midnight eastern time on the second Saturday before a scheduled meeting and ends at 11:59 p.m. on the day after the meeting. 

Other central banks follow similar practices. The ECB observes a quiet period beginning seven days before a monetary policy meeting. The Bank of England restricts Monetary Policy Committee members' communications for 8-9 days before the official rate announcement. The Bank of Canada restricts communications on monetary policy and the economic outlook during the week before the rate decision.

Before the blackout, policymakers' speeches can provide clues about their views on inflation, growth and upcoming interest rate decisions. For example, high ranking officials can correct a mispricing in the markets by signalling the most likely outcome of an upcoming meeting to avoid surprises that generally lead to high volatility. 

However, the blackout period does not prevent markets from pricing in a different outcome. An unexpectedly hot inflation report or employment release can still significantly change interest rate expectations. For example, the higher than expected inflation expectations in the University of Michigan survey released during the blackout period, infamously led the Fed to hike by 75 bps in June 2022.

After the blackout ends, policymakers can resume public commentary. Their speeches may provide further insight into the decision and the outlook for future policy. The policy announcement, accompanying statement and press conference remain the main sources of information. Subsequent speeches can help clarify the committee's reaction to new economic developments.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Market outlook for the week of 26th-30th October
item.description:
Monday will be relatively quiet, with no significant scheduled events for the FX market, but the rest of the week will be packed with economic announcements.

On Tuesday, Japan will release the BoJ Core CPI y/y, while the U.S. will publish durable goods orders m/m, the CB consumer confidence, and new home sales.

On Wednesday, Australia will release inflation data, after which the focus will shift to the RBNZ monetary policy announcement in New Zealand. In the U.K., the annual Budget will be released, while Canada will announce its monetary policy decision. Meanwhile, in the U.S., markets will focus on the highly anticipated FOMC meeting.

On Thursday, the U.S. will release its advance GDP q/q figure, the core PCE price index m/m, and unemployment claims. The ECB will also announce its monetary policy decision for the Eurozone.

Finally, on Friday, Japan will release the Tokyo Core CPI y/y, followed by the BoJ monetary policy announcement.

Traders should remember that Europe switched back to standard time on Sunday, and should also keep an eye on the month-end rebalancing, which could contribute to market volatility.

In Australia, the consensus for the monthly CPI is 0.7% vs. 0.4% prior and for CPI y/y it's 4.2%, up from 4.0% previously. The trimmed mean CPI is forecasted to print 0.3% m/m compared to 0.2% previously.

Westpac analysts expect a slightly cooler monthly print, forecasting September CPI to rise 0.6% m/m, lifting the monthly annual pace to 4.1% y/y. The largest monthly gains are expected from recreation and culture, followed by transport.

On the quarterly series, Westpac expects Q3 CPI to rise 1.3% q/q, keeping the quarterly annual rate steady at 3.9% y/y. The underlying inflation is projected to remain elevated with the trimmed mean expected to rise 0.9% q/q, while Westpac's monthly trimmed mean for September is 0.3%, holding the annual rate at 3.6% for a fourth consecutive month.

At this week's meeting, the RBNZ is expected to deliver a 25 bps rate hike, lifting the OCR to 3.00%. Markets are pricing in further increases even though inflation data printed softer than expected.

According to the latest outlook, higher oil prices, a weaker NZ dollar, and resilient economic growth have raised the risk of inflation exceeding 4% in the fourth quarter. Recent comments from RBNZ officials have reinforced expectations for an October hike, taking a hawkish tone.

Analysts from ING believe the tightening cycle could prove even more prolonged, with an additional hike in December or February depending on incoming data. They project a terminal rate of 3.25%–3.50%.

For this week's BoC meeting, the consensus is for a 25 bps rate increase, taking the overnight rate to 2.50%. The odds of a hike are above 80% following the latest comments from Governor Tiff Macklem, who stressed that elevated oil prices pose inflation risks.

However, analysts from Wells Fargo believe that a softer-than-expected September inflation, easing underlying price pressures, and a weakening labour market could make the case for holding rates unchanged.

Meanwhile Scotiabank analysts believe the hike is already largely priced into the swap market, so the CAD's reaction will depend more on the BoC's forward guidance than on the decision itself. Any hints of consecutive rate hikes could provide further support for the Canadian dollar.

Looking further ahead, markets are pricing in around 100 basis points of cumulative tightening by the end of 2027, despite limited evidence that inflation warrants such an aggressive response. This leaves the CAD vulnerable to disappointment if upcoming data or the BoC's decisions fail to meet the market's hawkish expectations.

In the U.S., the Fed is expected to keep the federal funds rate unchanged. Since the last meeting, inflation data has surprised to the upside, but recent FOMC member comments hinted that policymakers would prefer to wait before making another move.

This week's meeting is unlikely to bring any surprises, and since we won't get updated economic projections or a dot plot, there's also a good chance there won't be any changes in the policy statement.

Fed Chair Warsh is unlikely to deliver clear guidance on the path ahead, but he may strike a hawkish tone given elevated inflation data, ahead of a potential hike in December. Another thing to watch is the Fed's internal task forces, which are expected to present their findings around year-end, so they could get some attention in the coming months.

At its own meeting this week, the ECB is also expected to keep rates unchanged at 2.50%. The current political and fiscal situation in France is putting pressure on further policy decisions, as it drives borrowing costs higher.

Inflation in the Eurozone remains a cause for concern, sitting above the 2% target, with headline inflation printing 3.8% in September and core inflation sitting at 2.5%. Economic growth is projected to remain resilient in Q3, which would support future rate hikes.

Analysts from Wells Fargo expect a rate hike in December, but that depends on what happens with the bond markets. A French fiscal fix would give some breathing room, but if the bonds sell-off turns disorderly and impacts the Eurozone's other heavily indebted members, a hike becomes less likely.

In the U.S., the consensus for the core PCE price index m/m is 0.3% vs. 0.2% prior; for personal income m/m it is 0.3% compared to 0.2%, and for personal spending m/m it is 0.6% vs. 0.9% previously.

Consumer spending is likely to remain resilient, supported by continued growth in both goods and services consumption and personal income is also likely to show an increase. Wells Fargo analysts note that stronger income revisions and rising household wealth continue to support spending despite the high borrowing costs and persistent inflation.

The report will be released after the FOMC meeting, so it may not cause too much volatility, with the market's focus staying mainly on inflation data.

The U.S. advance GDP q/q will also be released this week, and the consensus is 3.2% vs. 2.2% prior, with the increase driven by consumer spending and business investment, especially in the high-tech sector.

Wells Fargo analysts argue that even though consumer spending may moderate in the near future, firmer income fundamentals will allow households to keep supporting growth in the coming months.

At this week's meeting, the BoJ is widely expected to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.25% to assess the impact of the 25 bps hike it delivered at the last meeting.

Inflation remains a cause for concern, sitting above the Bank's 2% target, and financial conditions are described as accommodative, which leaves room for further tightening. Traders will be monitoring the BoJ's updated forecasts, along with the Tokyo inflation data due for release on Friday. The consensus for the Tokyo core CPI y/y is 2.6%, down from 2.7%.

The Bank is expected to continue its hiking cycle in the future, with Wells Fargo analysts expecting the next hike in December and another one in 2027. Meanwhile, analysts from ING forecast the next hikes for January and April. Both expect the rate to reach 1.75% next year.

This article was written by Gina Constantin at investinglive.com.

item.title: Stock earnings pick of the week: Can Microsoft's AI growth still justify its spending spree?
item.description:
Microsoft will report earnings on Wednesday, 28 October, and once again this will be one of those times where the numbers themselves might not be the biggest story.

Now, don't get me wrong. The results will still matter. Analysts are expecting revenue of around $90.6 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, alongside EPS of $4.71. Those are strong growth numbers, especially when you consider just how big Microsoft already is.

But as has been the case with most big tech earnings, investors will be paying much closer attention to what management has to say about Microsoft's AI ambitions more than anything else. And that will particularly be the case after the recent selloff in tech stocks over the past two weeks.

Microsoft is already spending an extraordinary amount of money to build out its AI infrastructure. The firm's capital expenditure, including finance leases, hit roughly $41 billion in the previous quarter and management expects that figure to exceed $50 billion this quarter. Just think about that for a moment. We're talking about more than $50 billion in spending over three months alone.

Of course, Microsoft has good reasons to be investing so aggressively. Azure revenue grew 43% year-on-year in the previous quarter, with management guiding for roughly 45% growth in constant currency this quarter. Besides, the underlying backdrop signals that demand remains strong enough that available computing capacity is still struggling to keep up. As such, I don't think anyone is seriously questioning the notion of whether businesses want more AI computing power. The demand is clearly there.

Instead, the main concern is how much Microsoft has to keep spending to satisfy that demand and whether the returns will eventually justify the investment.

The fact of the matter is that building data centres and buying advanced chips isn't cheap. And while those investments can support years of growth down the line at some point in the future, they also come with substantial costs that investors cannot simply ignore forever at the present time.

As the market focus continues to revolve around that now, I would be closely watching Azure's growth outlook, cloud margins and any changes to Microsoft's capital expenditure plans this week. And considering how sensitive the tech sector has been in recent weeks, the implications could stretch well beyond Microsoft.

If Azure growth continues to impress and investors get greater confidence over future returns, that could help calm some of the nerves surrounding the broader AI trade. In particular, semiconductor companies and data centre operators would certainly welcome that reassurance.

But if spending keeps accelerating while profit margins struggle to keep up, investors will once again start questioning the economics of the AI boom more aggressively.

I don't think anyone is doubting Microsoft's capacity to once again deliver another strong quarter. The company has given investors plenty of reasons to expect one and amid the lofty expectations among big tech, posting blockbuster earnings these days seem to be the norm.

The only issue now that I'm seeing is that strong earnings alone may not be enough to appease investors. The market already knows that AI demand is booming. And so the focus has now clearly shifted to looking for evidence that all the money being spent to capture that demand will eventually pay off. And Microsoft's earnings will be another test of that very shift in sentiment.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Gold price tests $4,000 support, is a deeper correction looming?
item.description:
Gold is finding itself in a rather troubling spot to kick start the new week as we see price continue to test a potential break below the $4,000 mark. Looking at the chart, this will be a rather important test for buyers if they are to try and hold on to some semblance of hope for a rebound in ending October trading.

Despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and the recent retreat in Treasury yields, gold has struggled to find much upside traction lately. The rebound in August and September has faded completely and we're now seeing a pattern of lower highs, lower lows develop as sellers gradually regain the upper hand.

The $4,000 level is still holding for now, with price hovering around $4,007. So, I wouldn't go as far as calling this a confirmed technical breakdown just yet. However, repeated tests of a major support level such as this one without a convincing rebound would not exactly be encouraging either.

The swing lows around $3,942-60 will provide some additional layer of defense to the $4,000 mark for now. However, a firm break below the figure level and especially a convincing daily close below that could be enough to trigger further downside momentum in the precious metal.

And that could pave the way for a deeper correction towards the 100-week moving average, seen currently around $3,870. That is a particularly important technical level in my view as gold has not tested its 100-week moving average since October 2023. Besides that, the key level also sits near the October to November 2025 lows. As such, that makes the region a potentially significant area for buyers to regroup should selling pressure intensify.

For now though, the immediate challenge for gold buyers is to keep price above $4,000 and build a more convincing recovery. The first upside hurdle is getting back above the 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages, seen at $4,076 and $4,114 respectively. After which, getting back above $4,117 and the much difficult $4,200 level would offer some encouragement that the downside momentum is beginning to ease. But until then, I would argue that the balance of risks remains tilted to the downside for gold.

The only bright spot for buyers now is that this is a chart that has not actually broken down yet. The $4,000 mark is where the real test lies in identifying between that and perhaps a market that is vulnerable but still has the potential to recover. It's all down to whether buyers can hold the figure level as such.

item.title: Heads up: European daylight saving time has ended, here's what traders need to know
item.description:
This is just a quick heads up for traders before we get too far into the new trading week. If you're wondering why European markets seem to be opening a little later than usual today, well it is because we're back to that time of the year again.

Daylight saving time ended across most of Europe over the weekend, with clocks moving back one hour on Sunday, 25 October. That means the UK is now back on GMT time, while much of continental Europe has switched to CET time.

For those of you trading from outside Europe, particularly in Asia, this means European market openings and economic data releases will now arrive one hour later on your local clock. For example, the London stock market will now open at 16:00 in Singapore and Hong Kong instead of 15:00 previously.

But here's the other little wrinkle to keep in mind. The US hasn't made the switch just yet.

US clocks will only move back on Sunday, 1 November. So for this week at least, the time difference between London and New York is temporarily four hours instead of the usual five hours. That also means a longer overlap between London and New York trading sessions this week, something worth keeping in mind for those watching forex liquidity around the US market open.

Anyway, there's nothing particularly dramatic here. It is just one of those small calendar changes that can easily catch traders off guard. So, let this be a friendly reminder to double-check your economic calendars, market opening times and trading schedules before jumping into the action this week.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: EUR/CHF rebounds from 0.9200 but is the worst really over for the euro?
item.description:
After a rough few weeks in October, the euro is finding a bit of reprieve against the franc since the end of last week. EUR/CHF is bouncing off the 0.9200 level towards 0.9245 today but this the start of a proper recovery or merely a breather before another leg lower?

For now, I would argue that the technical picture still favours sellers despite the latest bounce.

Looking at the daily chart, the pair has already broken below its trendline support from the March to May lows, the 100-day moving average (red line), and the 0.9300 level earlier this month. That puts buyers in a rather uncomfortable position, with the latter now acting as a key resistance level alongside the broken trendline.

Meanwhile, the hourly chart shows the rebound running into resistance around the 100-hour moving average (red line) around 0.9243 currently. The key near-term level has limited gains in the pair since last week and is now put to the test again, with the 200-hour moving average (blue line) near 0.9263 being the next hurdle.

To the downside, the 0.9200 level remains the key support level to watch. A firm break below that would expose the late June to July lows around 0.9175-80, potentially opening the door towards 0.9000 thereafter.

So, what exactly could drive the euro lower again from here?

The most obvious is France's fiscal and political troubles, which are still weighing heavily on sentiment. The France-Germany 10-year yield spread holding around 166 bps after hitting a high of 176 bps last week, the highest levels since the Eurozone debt crisis in 2011.

As things stand, French borrowing costs remain elevated as investors continue to question the country's fiscal outlook. And until those concerns ease, the franc will remain an attractive alternative whenever European risks flare up again.

For now, the bounce in EUR/CHF is certainly welcome for euro buyers. However, there's still plenty of work to do before we can label this as a meaningful turnaround.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Major central banks take centre stage this week but will there be any surprises?
item.description:
The central bank bonanza is back in town this week, with five big names lining up to announce their latest monetary policy decisions. After all the recent drama involving oil prices, bond yields, and the stock market, perhaps it is time for central bankers to have their say again.

Of note, we will have the RBNZ, BOC, Fed, ECB, and BOJ all on the agenda this week. And looking to market pricing, traders seem to have a pretty good idea of what to expect already from the decisions to come. So, the only question is will there be any surprises? Let's see.

The RBNZ will kick things off on Wednesday with traders fully pricing in a 25 bps rate hike. That leaves little suspense surrounding the decision itself, although traders will be watching for clues on whether policymakers are prepared to tighten further in December.

Then, the BOC will follow later in the day with markets pricing in roughly 83% odds of a 25 bps rate hike. The pricing reflects relatively strong conviction with just a bit of room for a potential surprise. But all else being equal, the central bank should deliver as expected this week. Perhaps the bigger question is whether another rate hike will be needed as policymakers continue to wrestle with inflation risks. So, that will be the key risk trigger for the loonie reaction in the aftermath.

After that, we will have the Fed to finish off the day with traders assigning around 91% odds of no change in interest rates. As such, the decision itself won't be the main talking point here. Instead, it will all rest on Fed chair Warsh's pess conference. His remarks will be closely scrutinised, especially with rising oil prices complicating the inflation outlook while recent weakness in the stock market raises fresh concerns about growth.

And on Thursday, it is then on the ECB to take the wheel with markets pricing in roughly 90% odds of a hold. But with energy-driven inflation pressures building and European growth showing signs of weakness, ECB president Lagarde will have a lot to address with her press conference. In particular, traders will be looking for clues on December, where expectations for another rate hike have been building.

Finally, the BOJ will round things off on Friday with traders seeing roughly 98% odds of no change in interest rates. But with the yen still struggling and underlying inflation holding near 2%, the focus will be on whether policymakers offer any stronger signals about a potential move in December. BOJ governor Ueda's press conference is likely to steer clear of any pre-commitment though, so there might not be much to the key risk event here; all else being equal.

All things considered, I wouldn't expect the interest rate decisions alone to deliver much drama this week. As we've seen time and again, it is often what central bankers say about their next move that ends up stirring markets the most. So, that is what I'll be watching more closely with the meeting decisions and press conferences this week.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • Oil gapped lower at the open after a weekend without fresh US escalation of the war, easing from near six-month highs, though continued attacks on Saudi Arabia kept supply concerns in focus

Oil

Oil prices opened with a gap lower on Monday after a weekend in which the US did not escalate the war with Iran, easing back from the near six-month highs reached late last week. Losses were limited, however, as ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia kept supply concerns in focus.

Fresh news flow was thin during the session. Later, two sources told Reuters that senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were expected to meet Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday to discuss regional coordination.

Separately, Saudi Arabia and Singapore said Saudi crude will be stored in underground caverns on Singapore’s Jurong Island from the second half of 2027, aimed at strengthening Asian supply security while Strait of Hormuz flows remain disrupted. Saudi Aramco is due to sign a memorandum of understanding with Singapore’s Energy Market Authority and Jurong Group, with talks targeted to conclude within months.

Gold

Gold hovered near a three-month low as investors awaited this week’s Federal Reserve meeting for signals on the US rate outlook. Elevated energy prices have reinforced expectations that the Fed will keep rates higher for longer, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. Gold fell about 4% last week and briefly dipped below $4,000. On the structural side, Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes in August, more than four times the pre-2022 monthly average, with some reserves shifting from New York to London.

FX

Currency markets were largely subdued, although USD/JPY showed some volatility within a modest range, moving from above 157.10 to below 156.75. China’s onshore yuan strengthened in early trade to its firmest level since June 9, 2022.

Equities

Regional stock markets were mostly lower, with South Korea leading the declines:

  • South Korea’s Kospi: down 1.6%
  • South Korea’s Kosdaq: down 2.8%
  • China’s Shanghai Composite: down 0.3%
  • Hong Kong’s Hang Seng: up 0.2%

In Tokyo, chip and electronics shares led the declines. Earlier, Goldman Sachs cut its 12-month Kospi target to 9,000 from 12,000, though it said the index still has more than 60% upside after a slide of over 35% from its June peak.

Brazil

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday, defeating right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro to secure a fourth non-consecutive term after trailing in the first round. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking the Bovespa fell nearly 15% in Asian trade on the result. Goldman Sachs said an extreme scenario on Monday could see USD/BRL rise 10%, long-term government bond yields climb about 200 basis points, credit spreads widen 30 to 40 basis points and Brazilian equities fall around 15%.

Other news

In Serbia, Aleksandar Vučić, who has served as both prime minister and president over nearly 12 years, conceded defeat to the student-led protest movement following Sunday’s snap parliamentary election.

In crypto, Strategy chairman Michael Saylor did not post his usual Sunday bitcoin chart, which has typically preceded the company’s purchase announcements. Some market watchers took this as a possible sign that Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, paused its buying last week, though the absence of a chart is not confirmation. Saylor was active on X, describing bitcoin as “the moat” in a reply to Jack Dorsey. The company’s Monday filing should clarify its activity, and its third-quarter results are due on Thursday.

Elsewhere, Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing for GPUs, and warned that tightening credit could force failures and consolidation among AI-focused neocloud providers. China’s commerce ministry said it reserves the right to take countermeasures against a proposed US Treasury rule widening curbs on American investment in Chinese technology.

Week ahead

It is a heavy week for central banks. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Bank of Canada are both expected to hike on Wednesday, while the Fed, also deciding on Wednesday, is expected to hold. The European Central Bank on Thursday and the Bank of Japan, which meets on Thursday and Friday, are both expected to keep rates unchanged. item.title: Brazil ETF tumbles nearly 15% in Tokyo after Lula’s comeback runoff win
item.description:
The Tokyo ETF move is an early and thin-volume signal, so the real test comes when Brazilian markets open, with the real, the local rates curve and the Bovespa likely to bear the brunt of any repricing. Goldman Sachs’ figures describe an extreme scenario rather than a base case, but they frame the scale of the potential move, with the long end of the curve and the currency most exposed. Positioning matters: markets rallied after the first round on expectations of a different outcome, so some of the selling may reflect that trade being unwound rather than a fresh view on policy. Spillover to other Latin American currencies and EM risk sentiment is possible if the selloff is disorderly, while a contained reaction could see dip-buyers emerge quickly.

---

Lula pulled off a rare second-round comeback, and the first verdict from markets, a near 15% drop in a Tokyo-listed Brazil ETF, suggests investors had been positioned for the other result.

Summary:

  • Lula won Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, securing a fourth non-consecutive term with about 52% to 48% and a margin of more than 4 million votes, with nearly all ballots counted
  • He trailed in the October 4 first round, making him the first candidate since 1989 to lose round one and win the presidency
  • A Tokyo-listed ETF tracking the Bovespa fell nearly 15% in Asian trade on the result
  • Goldman Sachs said an extreme scenario could see USD/BRL rise 10%, long-term government bond yields climb about 200bp, credit spreads widen 30 to 40bp and equities fall about 15%

Brazilian assets face a sharp repricing after President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won Sunday’s runoff election, with an early read from Asian trading pointing to heavy selling when local markets open.

Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro by about 52% to 48%, a margin of more than 4 million votes with nearly all ballots counted, securing a fourth non-consecutive term. The result marked a comeback: Lula trailed in the first round on October 4, making him the first candidate since 1989 to lose the opening round and go on to win the presidency.

The initial market response was stark. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil’s Bovespa index fell nearly 15% in Asian trade on news of the victory, according to Reuters. While trading in such offshore vehicles can be thin, the move offers an early indication of how investors may react across Brazilian assets.

Goldman Sachs set out what an extreme scenario could look like on Monday. The bank said the dollar could rise as much as 10% against the real, long-term government bond yields could climb by about 200 basis points, credit spreads could widen by 30 to 40 basis points and Brazilian equities could fall around 15%. Goldman framed these as an extreme case rather than its central expectation, but the figures underline the scale of the repricing risk.

Part of the pressure reflects positioning. Brazilian markets rallied after the first round, when Bolsonaro finished ahead, as investors priced in a higher chance of his victory. Sunday’s result reverses that assumption, leaving those trades exposed.

Attention now turns to the opening of Brazilian markets, where the real, local interest rate futures and the Bovespa will show whether the selling matches the scale signalled in Tokyo or proves more contained. Investors will also watch for early signals from Lula’s camp on economic and fiscal policy for the new term, which could help determine whether the initial reaction extends or stabilises. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia to store crude in Singapore caverns from 2027 as Hormuz disruption bites
item.description:
The arrangement will not add barrels before the second half of 2027, so the near-term price impact is limited, but it signals that producers and consumers expect Strait of Hormuz risk to persist well beyond the current war. Storage closer to Asian refiners would give Saudi Arabia a buffer to keep supplying key customers during future disruptions, helping defend its market share in the region against rival suppliers. Over time, a strategic stockpile in Singapore could reduce the risk premium Asian buyers pay during supply scares and strengthen the city-state’s role as a regional pricing and trading hub. For now, oil markets remain driven by the immediate disruption to Hormuz flows, which this deal does not address.

---

With the Strait of Hormuz no longer a safe bet, Saudi Arabia is planning to park its crude on Asia’s doorstep.

Summary:

  • Saudi Arabia plans to store crude in underground caverns on Singapore’s Jurong Island from the second half of 2027, the two countries’ energy ministers said on Monday
  • The announcement at Singapore International Energy Week aims to strengthen regional supply security as the US-Israeli war with Iran severely disrupts Strait of Hormuz flows
  • Before the conflict, about two-thirds of Asia’s crude came from the Middle East
  • Saudi Aramco is due to sign an MoU on Monday with Singapore’s Energy Market Authority and Jurong Group, with negotiations targeted to conclude within months
  • Singapore says the arrangement will boost the resilience of Saudi supply chains in Southeast Asia and its own energy security during disruptions

Saudi Arabia plans to store crude oil in underground caverns on Singapore’s Jurong Island from the second half of 2027, in a move aimed at strengthening energy supply security across Asia as the war with Iran continues to disrupt shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

The plan was announced on Monday by the energy ministers of Saudi Arabia and Singapore at Singapore International Energy Week. Singapore’s minister responsible for energy said the two countries had agreed in principle to set up the arrangement, which would make Saudi supply chains in Southeast Asia more resilient while also supporting Singapore’s own energy security in the event of supply disruptions.

Saudi Aramco is due to sign a memorandum of understanding on Monday with Singapore’s Energy Market Authority and Jurong Group, the state-linked developer of the island’s industrial estate. The parties aim to conclude negotiations within a few months.

The announcement reflects the strain the conflict has placed on Asia’s energy supplies. The US-Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that carries much of the Gulf’s crude exports. Before the war, about two-thirds of Asia’s crude oil came from the Middle East, leaving the region’s refiners and governments heavily exposed to any interruption.

Holding Saudi crude in Singapore would place supplies within reach of major Asian buyers, giving the kingdom a way to keep serving customers if Gulf export routes are blocked or delayed. For Singapore, already a major refining and oil trading centre, the caverns would add a strategic buffer to its energy system.

The storage will not begin operating until the second half of 2027, so it offers no relief from the current disruption. But the deal suggests that both producers and consumers are preparing for a longer period in which Gulf supply routes can no longer be taken for granted, and further arrangements of this kind may follow as Asian importers look to diversify their exposure.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman’s 79-tonne central bank gold estimate goes mainstream as reserves shift to London
item.description:
Heavy official-sector buying offers a structural cushion beneath gold just as speculative liquidation has dragged prices below $4,000, and it supports the argument that dips are being absorbed by long-term buyers. It does not guarantee a floor, however: near-term direction still depends on oil, yields and Fed expectations, and central bank demand did not prevent last week’s slide. The gap between Goldman’s flow-based estimate and officially reported purchases suggests accumulation may be larger than disclosed, which matters for the longer-run supply-demand balance. The shift of holdings from New York to London is a reserve-management story rather than an immediate price driver, but it adds to debate over the dollar’s role in official portfolios.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold dips below $4,000 as long liquidation swamps ETF buying, Saxo Bank says
  • Gold dips below $4,000 in worst week in four months as oil fuels Fed hike fears

---

While speculators dump gold, central banks are quietly buying it at a multiple of their old pace, and some are deciding they would rather keep it in London than New York.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, more than four times the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes a month, and up from its 44-tonne estimate for July
  • On a three-month seasonally adjusted basis, purchases are running at about 85 tonnes a month; China was the largest identifiable buyer at an estimated 25 tonnes, above the roughly 20 tonnes it reported
  • The estimate, first reported by investingLive on October 19, gained wider attention after Fortune highlighted it last week
  • Holdings at the New York Fed fell by 40 tonnes while those at the Bank of England rose 46; the Dutch central bank moved 86 tonnes out of New York and Ottawa to London
  • Goldman views central bank demand as a structural support for gold, even as prices have fallen below $4,000

Central banks are buying gold at more than four times their historical pace and shifting some of their holdings out of the United States, a trend first flagged by Goldman Sachs research that is now attracting wider attention.

As investingLive reported on October 19, Goldman Sachs estimates that central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, well above the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes a month and a sharp step up from the bank’s 44-tonne estimate for July. On a three-month seasonally adjusted basis, purchases are running at around 85 tonnes a month. China was the largest identifiable buyer, with an estimated 25 tonnes, above the roughly 20 tonnes officially reported by the People’s Bank of China. The findings were picked up last week by Fortune, which framed them as central banks quietly stockpiling gold at four times the usual rate.

Goldman builds its estimate from trade and flow data rather than relying solely on official disclosures. That helps explain why it runs well above the World Gold Council’s count of reported net central bank purchases for August, and it is consistent with the bank’s view that some buying, particularly by China, is running ahead of official figures.

The second part of the story is where the gold is held. Holdings at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York fell by 40 tonnes over the period, while those at the Bank of England rose by 46 tonnes, pointing to a shift in storage from New York to London. The Dutch central bank separately confirmed it spent six months moving 86 tonnes of gold out of New York and Ottawa to London. Those transfers relocate existing reserves rather than adding new demand.

Goldman continues to see central bank buying as a structural support for the gold market rather than a passing phase. That backdrop is notable given recent price action, with gold falling below $4,000 last week as speculative selling, higher oil prices and rate concerns weighed. The official-sector data suggest long-term buyers have kept accumulating even as short-term positioning has been unwound. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral
item.description:
With a hold widely expected, yen and JGB moves are likely to hinge on the vote and Ueda’s guidance. Hawkish dissent from Takata or Tamura, or language pointing to the next meeting, would probably bring December pricing forward and offer the yen some support. A unanimous hold paired with cautious messaging could see hike expectations drift toward January, keeping the yen soft. Front-end JGB yields remain the most sensitive gauge of shifts in timing, and Friday’s Tokyo CPI print lands on the same day as the decision, adding to the potential for volatility.

---

Earlier:

  • ING sees BOJ holding at 1.25%, two hikes in 2027
  • BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike

---

Ueda is in no rush to hike again this week, but he has made clear the BOJ is not done, with the debate now about whether the next move comes in December or January.

Summary:

  • The BOJ is expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25% at its October 29-30 meeting, after hiking from 1% in a 7-2 vote in September
  • Ueda has signalled that back-to-back hikes are not needed, but said that with underlying inflation close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and must stabilise it around target
  • The likely path is a hike to 1.50% in December or January, then 1.75% in March or April
  • Hawks Takata and Tamura may begin pushing for the next hike on Friday, setting up a possible move on December 17-18; dovish members Asada and Sato have dissented against recent hikes
  • Tokyo October CPI is forecast at 2.7% to 2.8% across the key measures, with September jobs, industrial output and retail sales also due

The Bank of Japan is expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at its October 29-30 meeting, with Governor Kazuo Ueda signalling there is no need for back-to-back increases but that rates will have to rise further toward a neutral level, according to Mace News.

The board raised the rate from 1% in a 7-2 vote in September. Since then, Ueda has said that oversized or consecutive hikes are typically reserved for situations where inflation is rising rapidly beyond target, and that the bank is making pre-emptive adjustments to avoid being forced into abrupt tightening later. Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, he said that with underlying inflation now close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and its main goal is to stabilise inflation around that level. Board member Junko Koeda also argued last week that the bank should not become overly cautious about raising rates.

Mace News sees the most likely path as a hike to 1.50% in December or January, followed by a rise to 1.75% in March or April. That would continue a faster pattern of tightening every three to four months.

The board is broadly divided into four camps. Hawks Hajime Takata and Naoki Tamura may start pushing for the next increase on Friday, setting the stage for possible action at the December 17-18 meeting. At the dovish end, Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato have dissented against recent hikes.

On the data front, Tokyo’s October CPI is forecast to show inflation at 2.7% to 2.8% across all three key measures, partly reflecting the fading impact of local fiscal support. September jobs, industrial production and retail sales figures are also due.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold dips below $4,000 as long liquidation swamps ETF buying, Saxo Bank says
item.description:
The split between fast-money selling and steady ETF accumulation leaves gold finely balanced: if long liquidation is close to exhausted, structural buyers could provide a base, but a decisive break of trendline support would likely trigger another round of technical selling. This week’s Fed decision and oil prices are the near-term catalysts, since any renewed jump in energy costs that lifts rate expectations would add pressure. A gold-silver ratio above 74 signals that markets are pricing industrial demand risk and broader de-risking, leaving silver more exposed if equities wobble. Speculative positioning has already been pared, which reduces some of the forced-selling risk from here.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold dips below $4,000 in worst week in four months as oil fuels Fed hike fears

---

Gold’s slide below $4,000 is a positioning story more than a fundamentals one, with speculators heading for the exits while long-term ETF investors keep buying.

Summary:

  • Saxo Bank said gold’s drop is notable because it came alongside a strong rally in US Treasuries, with momentum selling and long liquidation overwhelming the usual support from lower yields
  • Spot gold briefly fell below $4,000 after Thursday’s break of support around $4,060 accelerated technical selling, putting it on course for its steepest weekly drop in months
  • Silver fell toward an 11-month low near $54, pushing the gold-silver ratio above 74, also an 11-month high
  • ETF investors have kept accumulating gold almost uninterrupted since July, and Saxo Bank says the correction does not necessarily invalidate the longer-term case
  • Support sits at an ascending trendline near $3,985, with resistance around $4,060 and then $4,230

Gold’s slide below $4,000 an ounce is being driven by speculative selling rather than a breakdown in long-term demand, according to Saxo Bank, which said momentum-driven selling and long liquidation have outweighed influences that would normally support the metal.

The decline has been particularly striking because it has coincided with a powerful rally in US Treasuries, Saxo Bank said in a note. Falling bond yields would usually help gold, but this week the selling pressure has proved stronger. Spot gold briefly slipped below $4,000 during Friday’s Asian session after a break of support around $4,060 on Thursday accelerated technical selling. The metal was heading for its steepest weekly fall in several months and potentially its weakest weekly close since November, despite persistent geopolitical uncertainty and growing concern over the durability of the equity market rally.

Silver has fared worse, falling toward an 11-month low near $54. That has pushed the gold-silver ratio above 74, also an 11-month high, reflecting silver’s relative weakness amid broader risk reduction and worries about industrial demand.

Saxo Bank said the price action suggests short-term speculative selling is currently outweighing demand from longer-term investors, who have continued to build gold holdings through exchange-traded funds almost without pause since July, seeking protection against fiscal instability, currency debasement and geopolitical risk. A chart from the bank shows ETF holdings climbing back above roughly 100 million ounces, while speculative positions on COMEX have been pared back from recent highs.

The bank stressed that the correction does not necessarily undermine gold’s longer-term investment case, but said it shows that even assets with structural support can suffer sharp setbacks when speculative positions are unwound.

The focus now is on whether gold can stabilise. Saxo Bank highlighted an ascending trendline connecting the October 2025 and July 2026 lows, currently offering support near $3,985. The broken $4,060 level may act as initial resistance, ahead of a more significant barrier around $4,230. A lasting recovery is likely to require steadier energy prices, continued buying from central banks and ETF investors, and evidence that the recent wave of long liquidation has run its course.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
